parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āculus.

parole.significato: forms the feminine singular past participle of verbs whose infinitive ends in -ar
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese -ada, from Latin -āta.

parole.significato: forms the masculine singular past participle of verbs whose infinitives end in -ar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ado, from Latin -ātus, from Proto-Italic *-ātos, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos, from *-éh₂ + *-tós. Doublet of -ato.

parole.significato: forms nouns, from the names of types of professionals, meaning the position of being that type of professional; -dom
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātus, from -tus, -tūs, from Proto-Italic *-tus, from Proto-Indo-European *-tus (suffix deriving action nouns from verb roots).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -al, from Latin -ālem.

parole.significato: forms adjectives, from nouns, meaning “of, from or related to the suffixed noun”; -an
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ano, a learned borrowing from Latin -ānus, from Proto-Italic *-ānos, from *-nos, from Proto-Indo-European *-nós. Doublet of -ão.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ança, from Latin -antia, from -ius, from Old Latin -ios, from Proto-Italic *-ios, from *-ijos, from Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós. Doublet of -ância. Cognate with Spanish -anza, French -ance and Italian -anza.

parole.significato: -ate (derivative of a salt or ester of an acid whose name ends in -ico)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ātus (second declension), from Proto-Italic *-ātos. These chemistry nouns originated as substantivized perfect passive participles from first conjugation Latin verbs; e.g. the Latin adjective acētātus in the 18th-century Latin phrase plumbum acētātum (“lead acetate”, li
Learned borrowing from Latin -ātus (fourth declension), from Proto-Italic *-tus. Doublet of -ado, which is inherited.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -dor, from Latin -tōrem.
Inherited from Latin -ētum.
Inherited from Latin -iculus.
Inherited from Latin -īculus.
Learned borrowing from Latin -icus, which forms adjectives of belonging or origin, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikos, *-iḱos.
Learned borrowing from Latin -īlis.
Derived from Latin -īnus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ỹo. Compare Italian -ino, French -in, both diminutive suffixes. Doublet of -ino.
Borrowed from Latin -īnus (“-ine”). Doublet of -inho.
Inherited from Late Latin -ittus. Doublet of -eto, -ete, and -eta.

parole.significato: -itude; -ness (forms abstract nouns, from adjectives, indicating a state or condition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -tūdinem. Doublet of -idão.

parole.significato: Used to form adverbs from adjectives; -ly
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -mente, inherited from Latin mente. Compare Galician -mente.
From Old Galician-Portuguese -mento, from Latin -mentum.

parole.significato: forms masculine singular nouns and adjectives
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -o, from Latin -um.
Learned borrowing from Latin -olus.
Inherited from Latin -tor, from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr.
Inherited from Latin -or, from Proto-Italic *-ōs, from Proto-Indo-European *-ōs, from *-os + *-s.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives and nouns from nouns for body parts to indicate that someone or something has a big example of or a la…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ūtus. Compare Galician -udo, Spanish -udo, Italian -uto, and French -u.

parole.significato: denotes a reference or relation to something; -ian
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ūtus. Doublet of -udo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese -avel, from Latin -ābilis. Compare -able dialectally and in various other languages; e.g. Sicilian -àvili, for a similar morphology.

parole.significato: -ancy (the condition or quality of being the suffixed adjective)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -antia. Doublet of -ança.

Learned borrowing from Latin -tiōnem. The suffix is in many cases a semi-learned form partially borrowed from Latin to make new words, but also corresponds with the old inherited form that it was based on (as evidenced by words such as canção), which could also be -zão in some cases (e.g. razão, saz

parole.significato: forms nouns, from verbs, indicating a state or condition; -ence
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -entia. Doublet of -ença.
From Latin -ibilis.

parole.significato: added to adjective X, forms verbs meaning to make/turn X
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese a-, from Latin ad-.

parole.significato: ab- (expresses the idea of intensity, separation, opposition)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ab-.
Borrowed from Latin acerbus.
Learned borrowing from Latin agenda.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese agosto, from Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin Augustus. Doublet of augusto.
Inherited from Latin ācrus.
Borrowed from Latin alba (“white”). Doublet of alva. Compare French aube (“dawn”).

parole.significato: alb (long white robe worn by priests and other ministers)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese alva, from Vulgar Latin *alba, from the feminine of Classical Latin albus (“white”). Doublet of alba. Cognate with Galician alba, French aube.

parole.significato: battlement (indented parapet formed by a series of rising members)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin minās (“battlements”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese anno, from Latin agnus (“lamb”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós. Cognate with Galician año.

parole.significato: animus (the masculine aspect of the feminine psyche or personality)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin animus (“the soul, thoughts, intellect, ideas, will, thoughts, courage, etc.; the breath, life”), closely related to anima (“air, breath, spirit, life force”). From Proto-Italic *anamos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, from *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe”). Doublet of ânimo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese ano (“year”), from Latin annus (“year”), from Proto-Italic *atnos (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-nos-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”). Cognate with Galician ano, Spanish año, Catalan any, Occitan, French, and Romanian an, Italian anno.
Inherited from Latin ante.

parole.significato: apt (fitted or qualified to do something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aptus, perfect passive participle of apō.

parole.significato: to plough (to use a plough to open furrows)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arar, from Latin arāre, from Proto-Italic *araō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éryeti (“to plough”), from the root *h₂erh₃-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese arco, arquo (“arch, bow”), from Latin arcus (“bow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo- (“bow, arrow”).
Learned borrowing from Latin arguere.
Borrowed from Latin austrum (“south”).
Learned borrowing from Latin auxilium.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ave (“bird”), from Latin avis (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis (“bird”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis (“bird”).

parole.significato: used for the fractions (or equal parts) of a unit divided in more than 10 equal parts; -th
parole.testo: From the ending of oitavo (“eighth”), from Latin octavus (< Proto-Italic *oktāwos), from octo (“eight”), possibly suffixed with Proto-Indo-European *-wós. Sense 2 is a back-formation from centavo (“cent”, literally “one hundredth”), from cento /cem (“one hundred”) + avo (“-th”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese barba, from Latin barba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰéh₂, possibly from *bʰers-.

From Old Galician-Portuguese beber, bever (“to drink”), from Latin bibere (“to drink”), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Cognate with Galician beber and Spanish beber, Catalan and Occitan beure, French boire, Italian bere and Romanian bea.
Borrowed from Latin bis.

parole.significato: bis (shows that something is to be repeated)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bis (“twice”).

parole.significato: a donation of food traditionally given to the poor to mark an occasion
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vōtum (“vow”). Doublet of boda and voto.

PIE word  *gʷṓws Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese boi, from Latin bovem (“cow, bull”) (probably through a Vulgar Latin form *boem), accusative of bōs, itself a borrowing from some Osco-Umbrian language dialect, from Proto-Italic *gʷōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws. Compare Galici

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bõo, inherited from Latin bonus (“good”), from Old Latin duonos, earlier duenos, from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Doublet of bónus /bônus, a later borrowing. Compare Fala and Galician bo, Spanish bueno.

parole.significato: drunk; under the influence of alcohol
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bevedo, from Latin bibitus, from bibō, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti, reduplication of *peh₃-, or from *-eti. Cognate with Galician bébedo.

parole.significato: to fit (no matter if space or volume is left)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese caber, from Latin capere (“to take in, contain”), from Proto-Italic *kapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Compare Galician caber, Spanish caber, Italian capire (“to understand”) and Romanian încăpea.

parole.significato: cape (piece of land extending beyond the coast)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabo (“besides; nearby”), from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-. Doublet of caput, chefe, and chef.
From Latin catīnus, from Proto-Italic *katinos. By surface analysis, cado (“cask”) + -inho.

parole.significato: to fall; to fall down; to drop
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caer, from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre, from Proto-Italic *kadō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱad- (“to fall”). Cognate with Galician caer and Spanish caer.

From Latin calvus, in turn from Proto-Italic *kalowos, from Proto-Indo-European *klh₂wós, *kl̥H- (“naked, bald”). Compare Spanish calvo, Catalan calb, French chauve and, more distantly related, Sanskrit कुल्व (kulva).
From Old Galician-Portuguese campo, from Latin campus (“wild field”). Doublet of campus, a borrowing from Latin. Compare Galician and Spanish campo.
Borrowed from Latin cancrum. Doublet of câncer and caranguejo.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin caput (“the head”). Doublet of cabo, chefe, and chef.
From Old Galician-Portuguese carne, from Latin carnem (“meat”), from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”). Compare Catalan carn, Spanish, Italian, and Romanian carne.
Borrowed from Latin cāsus.

parole.significato: catena (series of distinct soils along a slope)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of cadeia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cego (“blind”), from Latin caecus (“blind”), from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed, blind”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cẽa (“dinner (evening meal)”), from Latin cēna (“dinner (evening meal)”), from Proto-Italic *kert(e)snā, from Proto-Indo-European *kert-sna, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *sker-. Compare Galician cea, Spanish and Italian cena.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cen, from cento, from Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

parole.significato: one hundred (only in compounds followed by lower numerals)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese cento, from Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

parole.significato: key (object that opens and closes a lock)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese chave (“key”), from Latin clāvis (“key”), from Proto-Italic *klāwis (“bolt, lock, bar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“nail, pin, hook - instruments, of old use for locking doors”) (possibly through an Ancient Greek intermediate). Doublet of clave, a lea

Earlier cheo. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chẽo, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Doublet of pleno, a learned borrowing. Related to words such as Galician cheo, Spanish lleno, Catalan ple, and, more distantly, English full.
Inherited from Latin clausa.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chão (“ground”), from Latin plānum (“level ground”) < plānus, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Compare Galician chan and Spanish llano. Doublet of plano, porão, piano, and lhano.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chão (“flat, smooth”), from Latin plānus. Doublet of plano, piano, and lhano

parole.significato: to split; to divide; to separate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scindere.
Borrowed from Latin cippus. Doublet of cepo.

parole.significato: class, kind (group, collection, category or set sharing characteristics or attributes)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin classis.
Learned borrowing from Latin clāvem. Doublet of chave.

parole.significato: cloaca (excretory and genital duct in bird, reptiles and fish)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cloāca.
Learned borrowing from Latin co-.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coito, from Latin coctus, perfect passive participle of coquō, from earlier *quoquō, from Proto-Italic *kʷekʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷeti, from *pekʷ- + *-eti.
Borrowed from Latin color. Doublet of cor.

parole.significato: column (a vertical line of entries in a table)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin columna, a collateral form of columen, from Proto-Italic *kolamen, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH-.
Inherited from Latin contrā.

From Old Galician-Portuguese coraçon, from Vulgar Latin *corāceōnem, derived from Latin cor, from Proto-Italic *kord, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr ~ *ḱr̥d-. Compare Galician and Spanish corazón, Mozarabic ڧرجون (qurəjūn).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin corpus. Doublet of corpo and cós.

parole.significato: to run (to move quickly on one’s feet)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese correr, from Latin currere (“to run”), from Proto-Italic *korzō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).

parole.significato: crow, raven (bird of the genus Corvus)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese corvo, from Latin corvus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂wós.
Inherited from Latin cavus (“hollow; concave”). Doublet of cavo.

parole.significato: thigh (part of the leg above the knee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coixa, from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cozer, from Late Latin cocēre, from Latin coquere, from Proto-Italic *kʷekʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”). Compare Galician cocer.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese crecer, from Latin crēscere (“to grow”), from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cruz, from Latin crucem (“cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”). Doublet of Curuçá and Crux.

parole.significato: peak, the highest point of a mountain
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin culmen, from Proto-Italic *kolamen, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH-.
Borrowed from Latin cancer. Doublet of cancro and caranguejo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cão, from Latin cānus (“gray”), from Proto-Italic *kaznos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱas-. Cognate with Spanish cano.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ceo (“sky; heaven”), from Latin caelum (“sky”), from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-. Cognate with Galician ceo, Spanish cielo, Catalan cel, Occitan cèl, French ciel, Italian cielo and Romanian cer.
Borrowed from Latin cūria.

parole.significato: damage (an instance or the state of being damaged)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dano, from Latin damnum, from Proto-Italic *dapnom, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnóm. The use in games is a semantic loan from English damage. Cognate with Galician dano and Spanish daño.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dar (“to give”), from Latin dare, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”).

parole.significato: date (point of time at which a transaction or event takes place)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin data, from Latin datus (“given”). Doublet of dado and dada.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁. Cognate with Galician de.
From Latin dē-.
Learned borrowing from Latin decentem.

From Old Galician-Portuguese deus (“God”), from Latin deus (“god, deity”), unusual in that it was derived from the nominative instead of the accusative (deum), from Old Latin deivos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Italic *deiwos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god, deity”), from *dyew-
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dez, from Latin decem (“ten”), from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dezembro, dezenbro, from Medieval Latin Decembrius, from Latin December.

parole.significato: showing or deserving dignity; worthy; honourable
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dignus, from Proto-Italic *dek-no-, from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ-no, from *deḱ- (“to take”).
Borrowed from Latin dīvīnus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dizer, from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”). Compare Galician dicir.

From Old Galician-Portuguese doer, from Latin dolēre, from Proto-Italic *doleō (“hurt, cause pain”), from Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁éyeti (“divide”), from *delh₁- (“cut”). Cognate with Galician doer and Spanish doler.
Alteration of dous, from Old Galician-Portuguese dous, from Latin duōs (“two”), from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.

parole.significato: to sleep; to be asleep (to rest in a state of reduced consciousness)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dormir, from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

From Old Galician-Portuguese duro, from Latin dūrus, from Proto-Italic *dūros, from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-ró-s (“long”), from *dweh₂- (“far, long”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δηρός (dērós, “long”), Sanskrit दूर (dūrá, “distant, far, long”).

parole.significato: and (connects two clauses indicating that the events occurred together, one after the other or without any special impl…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese e, from Latin et.
Learned borrowing from Latin ego (“I”). Doublet of eu.
From Old Galician-Portuguese en, from Latin in (“in”), from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”). Doublet of in.
From Old Galician-Portuguese en-, from Latin in-, prefixation of Latin in (“in, into”); compare em.
Inherited from Latin inter-. Doublet of inter-.
Learned borrowing from Latin equīnus, from equus (“horse”), from Old Latin equos (“horse”), from Proto-Italic *ekwos (“horse”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos (“horse”).
Inherited from Latin ex- (“out of”). Doublet of ex-.
Learned borrowing from Latin scāla. Doublet of escada (“ladder, stairs”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese escano, from Latin scamnum, from Proto-Italic *skaβnom, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ-no-m, from *skabʰ- (“to hold up”). Cognate with Galician escano, Spanish escaño, Italian scanno, Sanskrit स्कम्भ (skambhá). Doublet of escanho.

From Old Galician-Portuguese escrever, escrivir, from Latin scrībere (“to write”), from Proto-Italic *skreiβō, from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ- (“to write”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish escribir, Catalan and Occitan escriure, French écrire, Italian scrivere, Romanian scrie and English shrive

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espinha, from Latin spīna (“thorn”), from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”). Cognate with Galician espiña. The sense of "spine" or "thorn" was lost to espinho.

parole.significato: thorn (sharp protective spine of a plant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espinho, from Latin spīnus (“thorn-bush”).

parole.significato: stellar (of, pertaining to, or characteristic of stars)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stēllāris.

parole.significato: star (apparently fixed star that has its own light and heat)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese estrela /strela, from Latin stēlla (probably through an unattested regional Latin *strēlla), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. Doublet of Estela. Cognate with Aragonese estrela, Catalan estrella, French étoile, Galician estrela, Italian stella, Occitan estela,
Borrowed from Latin stipula (“string, straw”).
Learned borrowing from Latin aevum.
Learned borrowing from Latin factum. Doublet of feito.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Classical Latin fallere, possibly from Proto-Italic *falsō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el-.

parole.significato: family; nuclear family (a father, mother and their sons and daughters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin familia (“household, family”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fazer. Compare Galician facer, Spanish hacer, Italian fare.

parole.significato: federal, federative (of or relating to a federation, a form of government that divides a sovereign state into smaller,…
parole.testo: Derived from Latin foedus. The slang sense comes from homem federal.
From Latin findere, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).

parole.significato: fierce (extremely violent, severe, ferocious or savage)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ferox (“wild, untamed”).

parole.significato: fetus (human embryo after the eighth week of gestation)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fētus (“offspring”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fio, from Latin fīlum. Compare Galician fío and Spanish filo, hilo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese firme, from Vulgar Latin firmis, from Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).
Learned borrowing from Latin fīxus. Doublet of the inherited fito.
Learned borrowing from Latin flamma. Doublet of chama.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese flor, a learned borrowing from Latin flos, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰléh₃s, from *bʰleh₃- + *-s. Compare Galician flor, chor.
Inherited from Latin folium. Doublet of fólio.

[Alt: A meat ant feeding on honey.] Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *morwísder. Proto-Italic *mormīkā Latin formīca Old Galician-Portuguese formiga Portuguese formiga Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese formiga, from Latin formīca, from Proto-Italic *mormīkā, from Proto-Indo-European *morwís.
From Old Galician-Portuguese forno, from Latin furnus, from Proto-Italic *fornos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰr̥-nós, from *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).
Learned borrowing from Latin forum. Doublet of fórum.

From Old Galician-Portuguese frade (“friar”), from Latin frater (“brother”), from Proto-Italic *frātēr (“brother”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr (“brother”). Doublet of freire, bróder, and brada.
From Old Galician-Portuguese freixo, freyxo, from Latin fraxinus, from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”).
Learned borrowing from Latin frequentem.
Borrowed from Latin fruī.

parole.significato: to run away; to flee (to move away from something unpleasant quickly or suddenly)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fugir, from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with Galician fuxir, Asturian afuxir, Catalan fugir, Italian fuggire, French fuir, Spanish huir.
Borrowed from Latin fulgēre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fumo, from Latin fūmus, from Proto-Italic *fūmos, from *θūmos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós, from *dʰewh₂- + *-mós.
From Latin fundō, from Proto-Italic *hundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-.
Inherited from Latin furnus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese foron, from Late Latin fūrōnem (“thief”), from Classical Latin fūr (“thief”), from Proto-Italic *fōr (“thief”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰṓr (“thief”), which is derived from *bʰer- (“to carry”). Cognate with Galician furón, Spanish hurón, Catalan and Occitan fura, Fren

parole.significato: female (animal of the sex that produces eggs)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese femea, femẽa (“female”), from Latin fēmina (“woman, wife, female”), from Proto-Italic *fēmanā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(f.) one who is sucked; one who suckles”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”). Cognate with Galician femia
Learned borrowing from Latin folium. Doublet of folho.
Learned borrowing from Latin forum. Doublet of foro.

parole.significato: gens (in Ancient Rome, a group of people descending from a common ancestor)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gēns. Doublet of gente.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese golpella, from Latin vulpēcula (“fox kit”), diminutive of vulpēs (“fox”), from earlier volpēs, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl(o)p- ~ *h₂ulp- (“(red) fox”). Cognate with Spanish vulpeja, Asturian vulpeya, Catalan volpell, Occitan volpì
From Old Galician-Portuguese gosto, from Latin gustus, from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.
Inherited from Latin glūten. Doublet of glúten.

parole.significato: grain, seed of various grass crops
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese grão, from Latin grānum. Cognate with Galician gran, Spanish grano, and Catalan gra.
Learned borrowing from Latin generis.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aver, from Latin habēre (“to have, to hold, to possess”). Compare Galician haber. Cognate of Spanish haber, French avoir, and Italian avere.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ome, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese omẽe, from Latin hominem (“a human”), from Proto-Italic *hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰm̥mṓ (“an earthling”).
Learned borrowing from Latin horrendus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese oste (“host, army”) (with the -h- added back to reflect the Latin etymon), from Latin hostem (“an enemy of the state”), from Proto-Italic *hostis (“stranger, guest”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest”). Compare Galician hoste, Spanish hueste.

parole.significato: guest (person lodged in someone else’s house)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ospede, from Latin hospitem, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European root *gʰost(i)potis, a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. See also hoste. Compare Spanish huésped.

parole.significato: age (part of the duration of a being or thing between its beginning and any given time)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ydade, from Latin aetātem, from syncope of earlier aevitās, from Proto-Italic *aiwotāts, from *aiwom + *-tāts, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital energy”), from *h₂ey-.
Borrowed from Latin in- (“un-, not”).
Learned borrowing from Latin inter-. Doublet of entre-.

parole.significato: fasting (period of time when one abstains from food)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese jajũu, from Latin iēiūnium (“fast”), from iēiūnus (“hungry, abstinent”), from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”). Compare Galician xaxún, xexún, French jeûne and Spanish ayuno. Doublet of
Inherited from Latin iuvenis, from Proto-Italic *juwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwHō (“young”). Compare Galician xove, Spanish joven.

parole.significato: to jubilate; to rejoice (to be very cheerful)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin iūbilāre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jugo, from Latin jugum, iugum, from Proto-Italic *jugom, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm. The preservation of the -u- was likely due to metaphony.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese junto, from Latin iūnctus, perfect passive participle of iungō, from Proto-Italic *jungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yunégti, from *yewg- + *-né-.

parole.significato: free from sin and guilt; righteous
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese justo, from Latin iūstus (“just, righteous”), jūstus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese lago, from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”). Compare Galician and Spanish lago.
Borrowed from Latin lāmentum.

From Old Galician-Portuguese lei, ley, from earlier lee, from Latin lēgem, from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s < *leǵ-. Cognate with Galician lei, Spanish ley, Catalan llei, Occitan lei, French loi, Italian legge and Romanian lege.

parole.significato: to read (to look at and interpret written information)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese leer, from Latin lēgere. Compare Galician ler and Spanish leer.
From Old Galician-Portuguese leve, from Latin levis, from Proto-Italic *leɣʷis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light”). Doublet of léu.
From Old Galician-Portuguese livre, libre, from Latin līber, from Old Latin loeber, from Proto-Italic *louðeros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-er-os, from *h₁lewdʰ- (“people”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logo, from Latin locō (“in the place of, instead of, for”, ablative), from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”). Compare Galician logo and Spanish luego. Doublet of lócus.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lũa, from Latin lūna (“moon”), from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Cognate with Galician lúa, Spanish, Italian, and Occitan luna, Catalan lluna, French lune, an

parole.significato: light (medium within which vision is possible)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese luz, from Latin lūcem, from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“white; light; bright”). Doublet of lux. Compare Galician luz.
Borrowed from Latin lapidem (“stone”). Doublet of lápis.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lingua (“tongue, language”), from Latin lingua.
Learned borrowing from Latin locus. Doublet of logo.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūbricus. Compare lôbrego, probably a doublet.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūmen. Doublet of lume.
From Old Galician-Portuguese madre, from Latin māter, mātrem (“mother, matron”), from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Doublet of mãe.
Learned borrowing from Latin magnus. Doublet of manho, which was inherited.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese magro, from Latin macrum, from Proto-Italic *makros, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós, from *meh₂ḱ- + *-rós.
Borrowed from Latin male (“badly”).

parole.significato: stain, blemish, mark, spot (discoloured spot or visible impression)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *macla (probably through a variant with a nasal infix *mancla), from Latin macula (“stain, spot”). Doublet of the borrowed terms mácula, malha, mágoa, mangra, and maquis.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mar (“sea”), from Latin mare (“sea”), from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Compare Galician mar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mao, from Latin malus, from Proto-Italic. Cognate with Galician mao and Spanish malo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese meio, meo, from Latin medius, from Proto-Italic *meðios, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare the borrowed doublets médio and médium. Sense of "way" or "mean" from Latin medium.

parole.significato: minor, underage (person below the legal age of responsibility or accountability)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin minor.

parole.significato: my (belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of me)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese meu, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mil, from Latin mīlle, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”).

parole.significato: maize (seeds of the plant Zea mays)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese milho (“millet”), from Latin milium (“millet”). Compare Galician millo and Spanish mijo.
Learned borrowing from Latin minūtus. Compare the inherited doublet miúdo. Also doublet of menu, via French.
Borrowed from Latin mōmentum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese moor, maor, from Latin maior. Doublet of maior and major.
Learned borrowing from Latin mora (“delay”).
Borrowed from Latin mucus. Doublet of monco.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mulo, a learned borrowing from Latin mūlus, possibly from Proto-Italic *musklos, possibly borrowed from a substrate language. Doublet of mu.

parole.significato: fine; ticket (monetary punishment for a violation)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin multa.
Borrowed from Latin multus.
Borrowed from Latin macula. Doublet of mancha, malha, mágoa, and mangra.
Learned borrowing from Latin maximus.

parole.significato: mother (female who gives birth to or parents a child)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mãy, nasalization of earlier *mae < *made, child-speech forms of madre, from Latin mātrem, the accusative of māter (“mother”). Doublet of madre. Compare pai (“father”), which underwent a similar phonetic reduction from its root (Latin pater), but was not nasalized. Cogna

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mão (“hand”), from Latin manus (“hand”), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry). Cognat
Learned borrowing from Latin meritum (“merit”).
Inherited from Latin munus.
Internationalism, ultimately from Latin nāsus (“nose”).

parole.significato: born (having a character or quality from birth)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nātus. Doublet of nado.

parole.significato: nation (group of people sharing aspects of language, culture and/or ethnicity)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese naçon, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin nātiōnem, from Proto-Italic *gnātiō (“family”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese noite, from Latin noctem, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

parole.significato: our (belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of us, excluding the person(s) being addressed)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese nosso, from Latin nostrum (“our”), from Proto-Italic *nosteros.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nove, from Latin novem (“nine”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Compare Spanish nueve.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese novo, from Latin novus (“new”), from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos (“new”). Compare Galician novo and Spanish nuevo.
Learned borrowing from Latin nebula. Doublet of névoa.

parole.significato: first-person plural nominative personal pronoun: we
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese nos, from Latin nōs (“we; us”), from Proto-Italic *nōs.
Learned borrowing from Latin nū̆cleus (“kernel, core”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese odor (displacing collateral form olor), from Latin odōrem. Doublet of olor.

parole.significato: to milk (to express milk from mammal)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ordennar, from Vulgar Latin *ōrdiniāre, itself from Latin ōrdināre (or through a *ōrdinium), from ōrdō (“order, arrangement”), from Proto-Italic *ored(h)- (“to arrange”), of unknown origin. Compare Spanish ordeñar. Doublet of ordenar.
Learned borrowing from Latin ōrdinārius, from ōrdō (“row, rank, regular arrangement”, literally “row of threads in a loom”) + -ārius, from Proto-Italic *ored(h)- (“to arrange”), of unknown origin.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese osso, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os (“bone”), from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Galician óso, Spanish hueso, Catalan, French, and Romanian os, Interlingua, Italian, and Sardinian osso.

parole.significato: other (not the one previously referred to)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese outro, from Latin alterum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ŏva f sg (“roe”), from Latin ōva n pl (“eggs”). Doublet of ovo (“egg”), from the Latin singular ōvum. Compare Spanish hueva.

From Old Galician-Portuguese ovelha, from Latin ovicula (“little sheep”), diminutive of ovis (“sheep”), from Proto-Italic *owis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis or *h₃éwis (“sheep”). Compare Galician ovella, Mirandese oubeilha, Spanish oveja.

parole.significato: egg (cell that results from the fertilization of the female gamete by the male gamete)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ovo, from Vulgar Latin *ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum. Doublet of ova.

parole.significato: ecclesiastical priest (Christian clergyman who performs masses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese padre (“father”), from Latin patrem (“father”), from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”). Doublet of pai.
Inherited from Latin patrōnus (“protector, patron”). Doublet of patrão and patrono.

From Old Galician-Portuguese pay < *pade, child-speech forms of padre, from Latin patrem, the accusative of pater (“father”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”). Doublet of padre. Compare mãe (“mother”), which underwent a similar phonetic reduction from its root (Latin mater), and, in addit

parole.significato: relative (someone in the same family; someone connected by blood, marriage, or adoption)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parente, from Latin parentem (“relative”), from pariō (“to bring forth, to give birth to, to produce”), from Proto-Indo-European *perh₃- (“to provide”). By surface analysis, parir + -ente.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parte, from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.
Inherited from Latin pasco.
Learned borrowing from Latin patentem.

parole.significato: patron saint (saint who protects a specific place, group of people or profession)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin patrōnus. Doublet of patrão and padrão.
Derived from Latin pēs (“foot”).

parole.significato: skin (outer protective layer of the body of a person or animal)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pele, from Latin pellem, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pender, from Latin pendēre, from Proto-Italic *pendēō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”).

parole.significato: to think (communicate to oneself in one’s mind)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre. Doublet of pesar.

parole.significato: to weigh (determine the weight of an object)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pesar, from Latin pēnsāre (“ponder, weigh”). Compare the doublet pensar.
Borrowed from Latin pīlum (“pilum”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pinho, from Latin pīnum. Doublet of pino and pínus. Compare Galician piño and Spanish pino.
Borrowed from Latin plangere. Compare the inherited Old Galician-Portuguese changer; cf. also Spanish plañir.
From Old Galician-Portuguese porca, from Latin porca (“sow”), feminine of porcus (“pig”), from Proto-Indo-European *porḱ- (“young swine, young pig”).

parole.significato: pig (the domesticated farm animal Sus scrofa)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porco, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”). Compare Galician porco.

parole.significato: posterior (following in order or in time)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin posterior.

parole.significato: powerful (having or capable of exerting power, potency or influence)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin potentem.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pouco, from Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare Galician pouco and Spanish poco.
From Old Galician-Portuguese poboo (displacing collateral form poblo), from Latin populus (“people, nation”), from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”), maybe from Etruscan. Cognate with Galician pobo.
Inherited from Latin premere.

parole.significato: arrested; imprisoned (having been taken into legal custody)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese preso, from Latin prēnsus, variant of prehēnsus.

parole.significato: prime (having no factors except itself and unity)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prīmus, from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos.
Learned borrowing from Latin prīmōris.

parole.significato: honest, decent, virtuous (having strong moral principles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin probus (“good, virtuous”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prae-.
Borrowed from Latin prō. Compare with inherited por.
Borrowed from Latin proprius (“own”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese punno, puno, from Latin pugnus (“fist”), from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, *puḱnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.
Learned borrowing from Latin post.
From Old Galician-Portuguese põer (“to put”), from Latin pōnere, from Proto-Italic *pozinō. Cognate of Spanish poner, French pondre, Italian porre, Sicilian pùniri.

parole.significato: public (pertaining to the affairs of all people)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pūblicus.

parole.significato: a small jug with a globular body and a single handle, used for pouring liquids from one container to another
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pucaro, from Latin poculum, from Proto-Italic *pōtlo- (with the instrument suffix *-tlo-, that yields -culum, compare Sanskrit पात्र (pātra, “drinking vessel”)), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃- (“drink”). Compare bibo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quatro, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
Inherited from Latin quem (“what”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rabo, from Latin rāpum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese raiz, from Latin rādīcem, from Proto-Italic *wrādīks, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”). Compare Galician and Spanish raíz.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ramo, from Latin rāmus (“branch”), from Proto-Italic *wrād-mo-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rei, from Latin rēgem (“king”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“rules”). Compare Galician and Fala rei.
Inherited from Latin ripa.

parole.significato: river (a large and often winding stream which drains a land mass, carrying water down from higher areas to a lower poin…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rio (“river”), from Vulgar Latin rius (“river”), from Latin rīvus (“a small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós, from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move or set in motion”) and *-wós. Cognate with Galician río, Spanish río, Catalan riu, Occitan riu, French r
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese roda, from Latin rota (“wheel”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese roxo (“dark red”), from Latin russeus (“dark red”), from russus (“red”). Cognate with Galician roxo (“reddish-brown”), Spanish rojo (“red”), Catalan ros (“blond”), Occitan ros (“russet”), French roux (“russet”), Italian rosso (“red”), Sicilian russu ~ ruxu and Romanian r

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese res, from the nominative case of Latin rēs (“thing”). Cognate with Aragonese, Asturian, Catalan, Galician, and Spanish res. From Old Galician-Portuguese sagrado, from Latin sacrātus.
Inherited from Latin sapio.
Learned borrowing from Latin salūbrem.
Borrowed from Latin sānus. Doublet of são.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese santo, from Latin sānctus, perfect passive participle of sanciō (“consecrate, appoint as sacred”), from Proto-Indo-European *sān- (“healthy, happy”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese seda, from Latin saeta (“animal hair”), from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”).

parole.significato: to scythe; to reap (to cut with a scythe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese segar, from Latin secāre (“to cut”). Unrelated to secar (“to dry”), which is from Latin siccāre.

parole.significato: to follow (to go or come after in physical space)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese seguir, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre, from deponent Classical Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

parole.significato: saddle (seat placed on the back of an animal)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sela, from Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
Inherited from Latin servientem. By surface analysis, servir + -ente. Doublet of sargento.

parole.significato: to serve (to work as a servant for someone)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese servir, from Latin servīre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sẽestro, from Late Latin sinextrum. Compare Spanish siniestro. Doublet of sinistro.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sete, from Latin septem, from Proto-Italic *septəm, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese setembro, setenbro, from Early Medieval Latin Septembrius, from Latin September.
From Old Galician-Portuguese seu, sou, from Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé (“self”).
Learned borrowing from Latin signum. Doublet of sino, senho, senha, and sinal.
Learned borrowing from Latin sincērus.
Learned borrowing from Latin sinistrum (“left”). Doublet of sestro.
Inherited from Latin sub-. Doublet of sub-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sob, so, su, from Latin sub, from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo (“under, below”).
Inherited from Latin super-. Doublet of super-.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sobrinno, sobrino (“nephew”), from Latin sobrīnus (“maternal cousin”), from Proto-Italic *swezrīnos (“of the sister”), from *swezōr (“sister”). Cognate with Galician sobriño, Asturian sobrín and Spanish sobrino.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sono, from Latin somnum, from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos, from *swep- + *-nós. Compare Galician sono, Spanish sueño, Italian sonno and French sommeil.

parole.significato: sister (female member of a religious community)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin soror.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sorte, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Compare Spanish suerte.

parole.significato: status; standing (a person’s importance relative to others)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin status. Doublet of estado.
Borrowed from Latin suāvis (“sweet, pleasant”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sub-. Doublet of so-.

parole.significato: forms the titles of male saints whose names begin with a consonant (except H, which is silent)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese san, clipping of santo (“saint”), from Latin sānctus (“sacred”).
Learned borrowing from Latin socius. Compare Spanish socio.
Borrowed from Latin solidus. Doublet of soldo.
Learned borrowing from Latin tangentem.
From Latin tangere, from Proto-Italic *tangō, nasal infix present from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-.

parole.significato: canvas (piece of canvas cloth stretched across a frame on which one may paint)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tēla (“web; loom”). Doublet of teia (“web”).
From Latin tendere, from Proto-Italic *tendō, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese terreo, from Latin terrēnus, from Proto-Italic *terzeznos, from *terzos + *-nos.

parole.significato: your (singular) (belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of you)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tou, from Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos.
Inherited from Latin tonāre.

parole.significato: toga (loose outer garment worn by the citizens of ancient Rome)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin toga, from Proto-Italic *togā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg-.

parole.significato: to hamper, to hinder, to impede
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin tollere (“to raise; to take away; to destroy”).

parole.significato: to twist (to turn the ends in opposite directions)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre.
Borrowed from Latin trans- (“across, beyond, on the far side”). Doublet of trás and trans.
Learned borrowing from Latin trānsversus. Doublet of travesso.

parole.significato: triple (made up of three related elements)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin triplus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese tres, from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
From Old Galician-Portuguese tu, from Latin tū (“you”), from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂ (“you”).

parole.significato: tacit (done or made in silence; implied, but not expressed; silent)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tacitus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ubre, uvre, from Latin ūberem, from Proto-Italic *ouðer, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”). Doublet of úbere.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ũu (“one; a”), from Latin ūnum (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”). Doublet of uno.
Learned borrowing from Latin ūnus. Doublet of um.

parole.significato: to smear; to spread (to distribute in a thin layer)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese untar, from Late Latin unctāre, frequentative of Latin ungere (via its past participle unctus), from earlier unguere, from Proto-Italic *ongʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”).

parole.significato: bear (a member of the family Ursidae)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos. Displaced the inherited doublet usso.
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of bainha and vagem.
Inherited from Latin valla.

parole.significato: to be worth, valid or acceptable
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese valer, from Latin valēre, from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥h₁éh₁yeti, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule, be strong”).

parole.significato: entrenchment, ditch (a fortification constructed of trenches)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vallum.

parole.significato: vapor / vapour (the gaseous form of a substance)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vapōrem.

parole.significato: ford (location where a river is shallow enough to be crossed by foot)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vao, from Latin vadum (“ford”), from Proto-Italic *waðom, from Proto-Indo-European *wh₂dʰóm, from *weh₂dʰ-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vencer, from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, nasal infix from *weyk- (“to overcome”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vento, from Latin ventus, from Proto-Italic *wentos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts (“blowing”), present participle of *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

parole.significato: to see; to observe (to perceive with one’s eyes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese veer, from Latin vidēre (“to see”), from Proto-Italic *widēō (“I see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese verbo, vervo, from Latin verbum (“word, verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vermen, vermẽe, from Proto-Romance *verminem, from Latin vermis.
From Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).
From Latin vertere, from Proto-Italic *wertō, from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.

From Old Galician-Portuguese verão (“spring”), from Vulgar Latin *veranum (tempus), from Latin vēr (“spring”), from earlier *veror, from Proto-Italic *wezor, from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥ (“spring”). Compare Galician verán, Spanish verano and Romanian vară.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese via, from Latin via, from Proto-Italic *wiā, from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vida, from Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vide, from Latin vītis (“a grapevine, or any vine”), from Proto-Italic *wītis, from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis (“that which twines or bends; branch, switch”), from *weh₁y- (“to twine, wind”) + *-tis (abstract or action suffix).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vinho, from Latin vīnum (compare Galician viño, Spanish and Italian vino, Catalan vi, French and Romanian vin, and English wine), from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.
Borrowed from Latin vītis (“grapevine”). Doublet of vide.
From Old Galician-Portuguese viver, from Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vivo, from Latin vīvus, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós.

parole.significato: widow (a woman whose husband has died)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese viuva, from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Classical Latin vidua (“widow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂. Displaced Old Portuguese collateral form viuda, from the same Classical Latin word.

parole.significato: widowed (said of a person who is in a state of widowhood)
parole.testo: From Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.
Inherited from Latin vōs.

parole.significato: your (plural) (belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of you)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese vosso, from Latin vostrum, from earlier vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.
From Old Galician-Portuguese voz, from Latin vōcem, from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs.
Borrowed from Latin varius. Doublet of veiro.
From Old Galician-Portuguese veo, from Latin vēlum, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *weg (“to weave a web”) or *weǵʰ- (“to ride”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin vīrus (“virus”).
Borrowed from Latin acer.

From Old Galician-Portuguese agua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”). Cognate with Galician auga, Spanish agua, Catalan aigua, Occitan aiga, French eau, Italian acqua and Romanian apă.
Borrowed from Latin apex, apicem.
Learned borrowing from Latin aureus (“golden”), from aurum (“gold”), from Proto-Italic *auzom.

parole.significato: cheer up (word of encouragement to someone who is unhappy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin animus (“the soul, thoughts, intellect, ideas, will, thoughts, courage, etc.; the breath, life”), from Proto-Italic *anamos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, from *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe”). Doublet of animus, related to alma (“soul”) and anima (“anima”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ānus. Doublet of anel.
Borrowed from Latin integrum. Doublet of inteiro.
Learned borrowing from Latin odium.
Learned borrowing from Latin onus.

parole.significato: bus (motor vehicle for transporting large numbers of people)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin omnibus (“for everyone”), dative plural of omnis (“all”). Doublet of omnibus.
Learned borrowing from Latin ultimus.
